title: xAI ships Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0, holds batch price at $0.10 per audio hour
subtitle: The new speech-to-text model is twice as accurate as version 1.0 and ranks first among 32 streaming models on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard — without a price hike.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: xAI released Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 on September 18, its second-generation speech-to-text model, and kept batch pricing flat at $0.10 per hour of audio. The company said the new model is roughly twice as accurate as Grok Voice Transcribe 1.0 and now ranks first for accuracy among 32 streaming models on the public Artificial Analysis leaderboard. The model is built on the audio foundation model that already powers Grok Voice inside the Grok assistant, Tesla in-car voice, and the customer-support call systems xAI licenses to enterprise buyers.

The interesting part is not the leaderboard — it is what did not change. Speech-to-text has been in a price war for two years, and every accuracy jump has usually come with either a token surcharge or a rate-limit tightening. xAI held the batch price steady and made the streaming tier the marquee accuracy claim, which is the harder of the two problems: streaming has to commit to a transcript before the sentence is finished. The model was trained on live, noisy, multilingual audio and refined with post-training against real dispatch, support, and vehicle recordings.

Voice is quietly becoming the highest-volume modality inside frontier labs. xAI said Grok Voice already transcribes millions of hours of narration a day and runs tens of thousands of concurrent support calls. OpenAI shipped its GPT-Realtime 2.1 voice agents in July, Google put voice into production for Gemini 3.8 Live extended thinking last week, and Anthropic's Claude for support workflows now defaults to voice on enterprise deployments. The competitive frame is no longer whether an assistant can hear you — it is who can hear a warehouse floor, a car with the windows down, or a call center at 2 a.m. without asking you to repeat yourself.

Takeaway for learners — when evaluating a transcription model for your own work, run it on your own audio, not the vendor's demo clip. The gap between a scripted studio recording and a real user on a phone with wind noise is where models actually fail. If you can afford it, keep a private 30-minute corpus of your worst audio (accents you care about, background noise you actually have, jargon your users use) and re-run it every time a vendor announces a new version. That is a more honest benchmark than any leaderboard.
